title: Den of Thieves
author: James B. Stewart

hero.description: A reading room for the people, deals and investigations behind an era of financial excess.

intro: Den of Thieves follows the 1980s Wall Street insider-trading investigations through financiers and the people pursuing them. Stewart draws on interviews, trading records and grand-jury material. Begin with the people rather than the jargon: who knows something, who can act on it, and who is willing to ask how the advantage was obtained.

context.title: Read it as reported history
context.text: The central figures include Michael Milken, Ivan Boesky, Martin Siegel and Dennis Levine. Stewart traces their world through a narrative of money, access and investigation. Financial expertise is useful, but following the relationships is a good first foothold.
context.editorialNote: The final sentence is original reading advice.

context.title: A reporter behind the narrative
context.text: Stewart shared the 1988 Pulitzer Prize for Explanatory Journalism with Daniel Hertzberg for Wall Street Journal reporting. Columbia's faculty record describes his background in business journalism and identifies Den of Thieves as a book about Wall Street in the 1980s.

context.title: Publication and format
context.text: The book first appeared in 1991. The publisher currently lists a 1992 trade paperback, a 2012 ebook and a 2013 unabridged audio download. These dates identify formats; they do not by themselves establish a new revision or new material.

pathways.label: First encounter
steps: Choose print, ebook or unabridged audio.
Keep a simple list of names and institutions; add connections as they become clear.

pathways.label: Read the reporting
steps: Follow one transaction and note who has access to information.
Mark where the narrative shifts from deal-making to investigation.
Return to the book's documentation to distinguish an attributed account from an inference.
pathways.note: Original editorial reading advice; the publisher confirms interviews, trading records and grand-jury material as research sources.

pathways.label: Read together
steps: Choose one question about incentives and one about the craft of reporting.
Compare interpretations by returning to passages in the edition everyone is using.

deeperGuide.label: Deeper discussion — after reading
deeperGuide.spoilerNotice: These questions concern the book's investigation and consequences. Open after finishing if you want to preserve the discovery.
deeperGuide.editorialNote: Original discussion prompts, not a publisher-issued reading guide or statements of current law.

themes.title: Information and advantage
themes.text: Trace how knowledge passes between people and institutions. Consider how small choices accumulate into a system.

themes.title: Status and rationalisation
themes.text: Look for the explanations people give themselves, and for the social rewards that make those explanations easier to believe.

themes.title: Investigation as narrative
themes.text: Notice how the reporter controls sequence, access and perspective. Ask what changes when an event is revisited from another participant's position.

questions: Choose one transaction. Who knew what, at what moment, and how did that knowledge change the choices available to others?
Where does the book show ambition turning into an excuse? Which details make that transition persuasive to you?
How do friendships, professional loyalties and the desire for status affect decisions on both sides of the investigation?
Compare a deal-making passage with an investigative passage. How does Stewart change pace, perspective or the kind of evidence he presents?
Which turning point depends most on an individual decision, and which depends on an institution? Would a different choice have altered the chain of events?
After the consequences arrive, what questions remain about responsibility, market trust and the reader's ability to judge a reported account?
